# Weekly Sync 8/31-9/4 ---
"Hero" Data Curation Run Progress We currently have about 10T tokens of pre-dedupe data processed! This will be significantly lower after dedupe, but dedupe alone now takes many hours (days?) to run, so I don't have timely feedback about how much data we have post-dedupe. **Updated this morning:**
> [!TIP] > The run is about 15% of the way through and will finish in the next 2 weeks if I don't steal my compute for other experiments. ---
More principled FLOP estimation ## Inference FLOPs of the fast curation cascade **Estimate: 1.3e10 to 1.7e10 FLOPs per extracted document, 5.1e14 to 6.7e14 per WARC, and 4.0e21 to 5.3e21 for the 8M-WARC run (7,925,398 WARCs).** The low end charges each document its real token count; the high end charges the padded length the chip actually runs. ettin68 accounts for 98% of the total. | | Actual lengths | Padded lengths | |---|---|---| | Per extracted doc | 1.3e10 | 1.7e10 | | Per kept doc | 6.9e10 | 9.0e10 | | Per WARC | 5.1e14 | 6.7e14 | | Per kept token (ModernBERT tokens) | 5.1e7 | 6.7e7 | | 8M run total | 4.0e21 | 5.3e21 | The rest of this note explains how the numbers are produced. The deployed pipeline (`lpv11_fastpipe_v2_1_fused`) scores every extracted document with three classifiers in sequence: fastText, a pooled super-token transformer, and ettin68. Each stage only sees the documents the previous stage passed on, so the cost per document is an expectation over the stages a document reaches. ### Stages and reach rates | Stage | Model | Context | Condition to run | Share of extracted docs | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | fastText w640 | full doc | always | 100% | | 2 | pooled transformer (90M-doc ckpt) | 8192 | fastText prob ≥ 0.0048 | 58.2% | | 3 | ettin68 | 2048 | pooled prob in [0.079, 0.8883) | 20.1% | Of the documents the pooled model scores, 18.3% are accepted outright, 47.2% are dropped, and 34.6% go to ettin68. Overall, 19.2% of extracted documents are kept. Rates are measured from production catalogs (52 shards, 12,824 WARCs). Per WARC: 39,464 records, 38,560 extracted docs, 22,423 fastText survivors, 7,749 band docs, 7,413 kept docs. ## Expected cost per document ``` E[FLOPs per extracted doc] = c_ft + p_ft * E[ c_pool(min(L, 8192)) | passed fastText ] + p_ft * p_band * E[ c_ettin(min(L, 2048)) | in band ] p_ft = 0.5815 p_band = 0.3456 ``` Each stage's cost is averaged over the token-length distribution of the documents that actually reach it. Those distributions come from the 100k comparison sample, which stores every stage's score per document: we tokenize its deployment text with the ModernBERT tokenizer and apply the production thresholds. The sample's reach rates match production within two points. **How padding works.** Within a WARC, the scorer sorts a stage's documents by length, takes batches of 32, and pads each batch to the smallest bucket in (128, 256, ..., context) that fits the longest document in that batch. The last batch is filled to 32 rows with empty rows. Because batches are length-sorted, all 32 documents in a batch are close in length, so the padded cost is well approximated by charging each document its own bucket; simulating the real per-batch procedure on the sample gives the same mean within 1%. Padding raises the mean charged length by 1.37x for the pooled stage and 1.30x for ettin68, which is the gap between the two columns below and in the headline table. | Stage | Reach rate | Mean tokens, actual (capped at context) | Mean tokens, padded | Cost per doc, actual | Cost per doc, padded | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | fastText | 100% | 1,318 (no cap) | n/a | 2.0e5 | 2.0e5 | | pooled | 58.2% | 1,010 | 1,380 | 4.1e8 | 5.7e8 | | ettin68 | 20.1% | 608 | 792 | 6.5e10 | 8.5e10 | ## 8M run document counts (7,925,398 WARCs) | | Count | |---|---| | Docs scored by fastText | 3.1e11 | | Docs scored by pooled | 1.8e11 | | Docs scored by ettin68 | 6.1e10 | | Kept docs | 5.9e10 | For reference, 4.0e21 to 5.3e21 FLOPs is the 6ND training cost of a 1B model on 700B to 900B tokens. ## Caveats - FLOPs and chip time diverge. Measured chip time from the catalogs implies MFU of 0.1 to 0.4% for the pooled stage and 1.4 to 5.7% for ettin68. All-in, the run is 26.2 v6e-8 slice-seconds per WARC (about 58k slice-hours for 8M WARCs), which is 0.35% MFU against the FLOP total. - fastText FLOPs count arithmetic only. Its measured cost is 0.55 CPU-ms per document, mostly hashing and table lookups. - Token counts use the ModernBERT tokenizer, not the training tokenizer. - Reach rates are from the current ladder's crawl mix.
Conventions - Forward pass only; a multiply-add counts as 2 FLOPs. - Embedding lookups, layer norms, softmax, activations, and the pooling reduction count as zero. - Length `L` includes the two special tokens and is capped at the stage context. The padded variant rounds `L` up to the next bucket in (128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192). - Empty tail rows in a WARC's last batch are included in the per-batch simulation and add under 1%.
fastText formula dim 100, word bigrams, no character n-grams (read from the model header). Features are words plus bigrams, about twice the word count; words are taken as 0.75 of ModernBERT tokens. One add per dimension per feature, then a 100 x 2 output layer. ``` F = 2 * 0.75 * T c_ft = 100 * F + 2 * 100 * 2 ≈ 150 T + 400 ``` At T = 1,318 this is 2.0e5.
Pooled transformer formula Levanter's `PooledTransformerConfig.flops_per_token`, called directly. `L` padded tokens, `S = L / 64` super-tokens, hidden `D = 512`, pooled input width 768 (mean, max, min of 256-dim embeddings), feed-forward 2048, 4 layers, 2 labels. ``` proj = 2 * 768 * D * S layer = 2 * 4 * D^2 * S # q, k, v, o projections + 2 * 2 * S^2 * D # QK^T and AV + 2 * 2 * D * 2048 * S # MLP head = 2 * D * 2 c_pool(L) = proj + 4 * layer + head ``` About 4.1e5 FLOPs per input token, nearly flat in `L`.
ettin68 formula Hand-derived (Levanter's generic helper adds a vocabulary-head term a classifier does not have). Hidden `D = 512`, GeGLU feed-forward 768, 19 layers, 8 heads, global attention on every third layer starting at layer 0 (7 layers), sliding window 128 on the other 12. ``` linear_per_token_per_layer = 2 * 4 * D^2 # q, k, v, o + 2 * D * 2 * 768 # GeGLU up and gate + 2 * 768 * D # down attn_per_token_per_layer = 4 * span * D # span = L (global), min(L, 128) (local) c_ettin(L) = L * sum over 19 layers of (linear + attn) ``` Linear term 8.5e7 per token (two times the 42M non-embedding parameters); attention 3.2e7 at L = 2048; total 1.17e8 per token.
Data sources - Reach rates and per-WARC counts: fused catalogs, 52 random shards of the 404 to 8079 ladder. - Per-stage length distributions: 100k comparison sample (`extractor_compare/high_quality_200warc`), deployment text tokenized with `answerdotai/ModernBERT-base`, production thresholds applied to stored scores. - Model shapes: checkpoint `config.json` for pooled 90M and ettin68; fastText hyperparameters from the model binary header. - Chip time: catalog columns `pooled_s` and `score_s` times device count, per device type.
> [!TIP] > The distilled pipeline is projected to take about 5e21 flops to run on the full 8M WARC files. > The previous 8B model running on all of the internet was projected to take between 3e25 and 1.8e26 flops depending on if I used the pipeline version or the single call spec. > The fact that it is taking a month is likely somewhat due to poor MFU ---
Updated Main Results from Mixing
> [!TIP] > Finally showing signs of how the "more data" really helps at scale (100B+ tokens) ---
Beta Paper Outline Old Paper: https://www.overleaf.com/read/krtygrzdmrzc#9088c4 New Paper (extremely preliminary for now, will auto-update here): https://www.overleaf.com/read/tzzfngmmyqsp#daf616 **Introduction:** Something about how we should spend way more compute on data curation but it doesn't need to be more complicated. **Background**: Current data curation pipelines including data mixing **Method**: Spec-Driven Curation, as well as the distillation into FastText, Pooled Transformer, and Ettin68 (modernBERT) **Swapping the spec enables control of the data distribution**: We show different specs lead to expected changes in data downstream
Plots
We then argue that because of the mixing and the growing demand for tokens we opt to use the coverage spec. **Spec-Driven Curation Yields Bigger and Better Data**: We show that by using our high coverage spec distilled pipeline we get more data and can mix it to be better at many domains.
Plots **Bigger**: Everything else bends upwards, but we can train on 100B+ tokens from just 10k WARCs. If we 800x (which is a bad way to do this bc no accounting for dedup), then we should be able to train on 80T tokens without issue. **Better Coverage**: We can mix for several downstream target capabilities.
**Ablations**: When we remove parts of the system how much does it impact performance. All ablations will be done on the olmo base easy eval set.

issues.body:
PR #8748 adds object-backed Finelog storage. Its advisory lint review found follow-up debt outside the sparse-compaction rollout.

The highest-risk findings are:

- Kubernetes does not pass `object_cache_gb` into the container environment (`lib/finelog/src/finelog/deploy/config.py`).
- Boot reconciliation silently excludes invalid persisted object IDs (`lib/finelog/rust/src/store/table/controller.rs`).
- Provider and scan paths normalize object keys independently (`lib/finelog/rust/src/store/object_store/provider.rs` and `remote.rs`).
- Scheduler panics and failed staging-file cleanup can be discarded (`lib/finelog/rust/src/maintenance/scheduler.rs` and `store/object_store/local_file.rs`).

The review also found stale documentation, same-branch catalog migration churn, oversized recovery and registration functions, positional return tuples, duplicated test fixtures, and wall-clock sleeps in catalog, forwarding, migration, rollback, and cache tests.

Done when:

- Kubernetes applies the configured object-cache limit.
- Object IDs and object-store paths use one validated representation from persistence through scans.
- Scheduler and staging cleanup failures are reported without hiding the original operation failure.
- The catalog migrations contain no undeployed add-then-remove schema churn.
- The named documentation matches current behavior.
- Shared fixtures replace the duplicated policy and schema setup.
- Timing-sensitive tests use deterministic seams or condition-based synchronization.
- Recovery, registration, compaction commit, and test-support return values have focused interfaces.
- `./infra/pre-commit.py --review` has no remaining findings from this set.

Related: #8748

issues.body:
The advisory lint review for PR #8748 found cleanup work that is unrelated to the remaining object-native rollout. Track it separately so the rollout can finish without losing the findings.

The correctness-sensitive findings are:

- `maintenance/scheduler.rs` discards a scheduler `JoinError` during shutdown.
- `store/catalog/namespaces.rs` treats every SQLite lookup failure as a missing row.
- `store/legacy/archive.rs` can unlink a file after the catalog mutation fails.
- `store/table/controller.rs` skips malformed canonical object references during boot reconciliation.

The structural findings cover the add-then-remove catalog migrations; overloaded recovery/runtime constructors; repeated GC parameter groups and tuple returns; process-global rewrite state; ambiguous boolean compaction outcomes; the migration script's raw state dictionary; and duplicated protobuf decoding in `object_query_client.py`.

The test findings cover wall-clock sleeps and duplicate polling in forwarding tests, timestamp sleeps in catalog and store tests, and assertions coupled to human-readable error text. The prose findings cover trivial or implementation-narrating docstrings and transient issue-number comments in the store, index, and migration modules.

Done when:

- The four correctness-sensitive findings propagate or report failures without leaving catalog and filesystem state inconsistent.
- Catalog migrations on the unmerged branch contain no add-then-remove columns.
- The structural findings are resolved or explicitly dismissed with a concrete reason.
- Timing-dependent tests use deterministic clocks or event synchronization, duplicate polling is shared, and behavioral tests assert structured outcomes where available.
- Trivial docstrings and transient rollout references are removed or rewritten as durable contracts.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Analysis — no PR from `main`; this is branch-scoped cleanup on #8748.**

The issue is actionable (concrete files, concrete defects, explicit "Done when"), but every target file exists **only** on the unmerged object-native branch `agent/20260827-fix-8737` (PR #8748). `main`'s `lib/finelog/rust/src/store/` has a different layout with no `catalog/`, `legacy/`, `table/`, or `maintenance/` subtrees. A fix branched off `main` would reproduce the entire object-native diff and conflict with the live PR, so these changes belong in #8748 (or a branch stacked on it), authored by whoever owns the rollout. Root cause for the four correctness findings below; the structural/test/prose buckets are triage notes for that same branch.

**Correctness findings** (line links pinned to `95ecfce`):

- **Scheduler `JoinError` discarded** — [`maintenance/scheduler.rs` L112](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/95ecfce91723918d2527f59ebe0f7c41e7919420/lib/finelog/rust/src/maintenance/scheduler.rs#L112). `shutdown()` does `let _ = handle.await;`, so a panic in the poll loop is swallowed at shutdown. Match the join result and log/propagate the `JoinError`, ignoring only cancellation.
- **SQLite failure read as "no row"** — [`store/catalog/namespaces.rs` L190-L197](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/95ecfce91723918d2527f59ebe0f7c41e7919420/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/catalog/namespaces.rs#L190-L197). `query_row(...).ok()` maps any error to `None`, so an I/O or corruption failure looks like a missing row and `registered_at_ms` silently resets to `now`, rewriting the durable registration timestamp. Use `.optional()` (distinguishes `QueryReturnedNoRows` from real errors) and `?`-propagate via `sqlite_err`.
- **Unlink after failed catalog mutation** — [`store/legacy/archive.rs` L218-L229](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/95ecfce91723918d2527f59ebe0f7c41e7919420/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/legacy/archive.rs#L218-L229). `evict_segment` runs `let _ = catalog.set_location(...)` / `let _ = catalog.remove_segment(...)` then unconditionally `remove_file(path)`. If the catalog write fails, a `BOTH` row still reads `BOTH` while its local file is gone — the catalog references a local file that no longer exists. Gate the unlink on the catalog mutation succeeding and surface the error (the fn returns a bare `i64` today, so failures have nowhere to go).
- **Malformed object refs skipped in boot reconcile** — [`store/table/controller.rs` L861-L872](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/95ecfce91723918d2527f59ebe0f7c41e7919420/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/table/controller.rs#L861-L872). `sync_referenced_objects` does `ObjectId::parse(id).ok()` and `ObjectReference::try_from(source)` with `else { continue }`. A **live** segment whose canonical `object_id` is malformed parses to `None`, reads as "not object-layout," and is skipped — exactly the corrupted-metadata case the reconcile guard is meant to fail loudly on. Distinguish "not an object segment" from "malformed reference on a live object segment," and refuse publication (`Err`) for the latter rather than dropping it.

**Structural / test / prose** — defer to the branch author's triage: add-then-remove catalog migrations, overloaded recovery/runtime constructors, repeated GC parameter groups and tuple returns, process-global rewrite state, ambiguous boolean compaction outcomes, the migration script's raw state dict, and duplicated protobuf decode in `object_query_client.py`; wall-clock sleeps and duplicate polling in forwarding/catalog/store tests plus error-text-coupled assertions; trivial docstrings and transient issue-number comments. Each should be resolved or dismissed with a concrete reason, closing on a clean `./infra/pre-commit.py --review`.

**Proposed approach:** fold the four correctness fixes into #8748 (each is a few lines and locally testable against the branch's scenario suite), then work the structural/test/prose buckets as follow-ups on the same branch. Happy to take any single item once it can target the right base.

issues.body:
The advisory lint review of #8748 surfaced structural cleanups that were deliberately not landed in that PR's final commits. Each stands alone; none changes behavior.

Rust (`lib/finelog/rust`):

- `src/store/store.rs`: `recover_claimed_table` interleaves revision arbitration, retained-spec/schema resolution, segment-to-projection-row conversion, and local rebuild plus runtime re-registration; `register_table_with` runs name/schema validation, legacy spec derivation, TableSpec cross-checks, catalog merge, engine rebuild, and the spec-lifecycle commit in one body. Split each along those seams.
- `src/maintenance/scheduler.rs`: `schedule_maintenance` repeats `schedule_flush`'s dispatch scaffold (clone limits/wake/cadence/tables, permit, run_work, clear flag, notify, undo on failed dispatch). Extract the shared scaffold.
- `src/maintenance/mod.rs`: the `Cycle::pending` bit means a different thing per work kind (migration owns the cycle, placement pending, more compaction due), and scheduler.rs stores it as `migration_pending`. Replace with an enum.
- `src/store/compaction/object_driver.rs`: `(lease, active_version, migration_backfill)` rides three signatures with the first two only forwarded; `ObjectCompaction` already travels the same path and could carry them.
- `src/store/object_store/provider.rs`: `is_object_store` is false for a local directory this module serves through an `ObjectStore`; it tests for a remote bucket URL and should be named that way.
- `src/test_support.rs`: the resolve/Proceed match scaffold repeats verbatim in `write`, `read`, `upload_staged`, `local_path`, and `compare_and_swap`, differing only in the inner call.
- `src/store/store.rs` tests: a ~25-line open/register/build-batch/write/await preamble is copy-pasted across seven tests although `write_legacy_row` and `mem_store` helpers exist, and one test outlasts a 50 ms query bound with a real 200 ms sleep instead of controlling the clock.

Python client (`lib/finelog/src/finelog/client`):

- `object_query_client.py`: `pin_catalog` does checksum-verified object loading, HEAD/catalog identity and format gating, segment URI projection, and active-spec column mapping in one body, and it navigates the HEAD/catalog documents as untyped dicts via `_mapping`/`_integer`/`_sequence` although they are proto-JSON of `CatalogHead`/`NamespaceCatalog` with generated `stats_pb2` types available.

Two review findings are recorded here as intentionally rejected so they are not re-filed: migration `0006_drop_recorded_only_columns` dropping columns that migration 0002 added, and the reserved proto field slots in `finelog_stats.proto` — the intermediate schema and fields shipped to the live marin-dev catalog, so the ordered drop-migration and reservations are required.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
WHAT THIS IS: An experiment standing up THUDM's slime RL framework on Iris and doing some agentic RL with it on some TaskTrove datasets.

WHY WE DID IT: To sanity check MarinSkyRL against another well-regarded RL framework under similar training conditions.

WHAT HAPPENED: The experiment was largely a success. Converting THUDM/slime to consume TaskTrove data proved to be relatively straightforward; the repo is public at https://github.com/penfever/slime. Neither framework showed a definitive advantage in speed or holdout (val set) accuracy, although the training conditions were different enough to make direct apples-to-apples comparisons infeasible. 

CONCLUSIONS: While it is good to have slime as a backup option and sanity check, we will continue to use MarinSkyRL, as it is better adapted to our infrastructure and is more flexible in certain respects.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
# Qwen3-Coder Slime RL calendar sweep

## Objective

Train `Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct` with Slime on the immutable TaskTrove instruction-following calendar-v3 dataset. Produce sustained gains in unfiltered verifier reward without the intermediate collapse seen in historical MarinSkyRL R6.

R6 used an older dataset revision with an easier verifier. Its curve is useful for qualitative comparison only; its absolute reward values are not success thresholds for this experiment.

## Success standard

An arm is a winner when its real reward reaches at least twice its initial-policy baseline for two consecutive completed rollouts without a dramatic collapse. Real reward is the unfiltered verifier outcome before reward shaping, penalties, or sample selection. Slime numbers rollouts from zero, so rollout 0 is the initial-policy baseline when no separate pre-training evaluation exists.

When a run has a disjoint fixed evaluation stream, use its pre-training evaluation as the baseline and require two consecutive scheduled evaluations at twice that value. Training-batch reward remains a health and optimization signal, but it does not qualify the run because prompt composition changes between batches.

Both qualifying rollouts must retain mixed-reward groups and non-degenerate policy entropy. A later joint collapse in real reward, entropy, and mixed-group retention retracts the result; three or four noisy rollouts do not. Passing traces must use the current v3 verifier and may not rely on command-level access to hidden task or verifier state. Results dominated by pass-through termination, turn-cap exhaustion, missing behavior log probabilities, or failed verifier execution do not qualify. Reward reported only after dynamic filtering or other sample selection cannot satisfy this standard.

## Fixed contracts

- Dataset: `open-thoughts/TaskTrove@66942851ad1b59c28c830a1b1aba3ee9bb926acc::laion__nemotron-gym-instruction-following-calendar-v3` (5,673 tasks).
- Sandbox: Daytona snapshot `harbor__5da1af9a2eaf__snapshot` with workdir `/app`.
- Answer contract: transfer only `answer.txt` from the agent sandbox into a fresh evaluator sandbox. Verifier assets remain absent from the agent sandbox.
- Daytona credential: source `DAYTONA_RL_API_KEY` and expose that value to the job as `DAYTONA_API_KEY`. Do not use the generic key.
- Cluster: `cw-rno2a`; priority: `interactive`; H100x8 nodes.
- At most three concurrent RL jobs. This limit counts jobs, not nodes. The third slot is reserved for the user-authorized `2e-6` 512-task short-epoch arm; do not generalize it to another sweep expansion without a new decision.
- Model calls: at most 32,768 context tokens and 4,096 new tokens per turn.
- Record every attempted launch and every optimizer iteration in `TRACKER.md`.

## Initial search policy

Start with two separated five-node runs, each using 16 actor GPUs and 24 rollout GPUs (six TP4 engines). Use eight samples per prompt, 32 prompt groups per rollout, binary verifier reward, GRPO advantages, sequence-mean loss, zero KL, gradient clipping, and no dynamic filtering. The first pair varies only learning rate (`1e-6` and `2e-6`).

Run one additional five-node `2e-6` arm on a deterministic 512-task subset of the post-validation training pool. Keep every other optimization, rollout, sandbox, verifier, and fixed-validation setting equal to the full-data `2e-6` arm. With 32 prompt groups per rollout, one training epoch is exactly 16 completed rollouts. Mark every multiple of 16 as an epoch boundary and compare both fixed-validation reward and collapse ratios across epochs; repeated exposure does not relax the winner or retirement rules.

Historical runs show entropy concentration and informative-group collapse. Treat three to four noisy optimizer steps as normal search variance unless an arm crosses one of the quantitative collapse boundaries below. Absent a mechanical or data-contract failure, do not make another negative learning or termination verdict before five completed optimizer steps; the positive two-rollout winner criterion may be satisfied earlier. Continue an arm while it retains sufficient mixed groups and policy entropy, even when its short-term reward trails the other arm. Stop and diagnose if completed trials consistently lack verifier outcomes, all rollout groups become uniform and eliminate the learning signal, the trainer stops banking steps, either quantitative boundary persists for three consecutive valid measurements, or a five-step window jointly shows sustained deterioration in mixed-group retention, real reward, and entropy. If both initial arms eventually meet a collapse signature, keep the better learning rate and introduce entropy regularization in the next pair rather than increasing learning rate.

Use mixed-reward-group retention together with real reward and policy entropy as the leading health signal. Define the mixed-group ratio as `mixed groups / configured prompt groups`; for the current 32-group runs, compute it as `(32 - all-zero groups - all-one groups) / 32`. Its floor is `1/8`. Exactly four mixed groups in a 32-group rollout is at the floor. Fewer than four is below it. Retire an arm after three consecutive completed rollouts below the floor. A rollout at or above the floor resets this counter.

Define entropy retention as `optimizer entropy / initial-policy entropy`, using optimizer step 0 from the same arm as the initial-policy reference. Its floor is `1/5`. Retire an arm after three consecutive completed optimizer steps below this floor. A step at or above the floor resets this counter. Do not compare absolute entropy across arms or configurations with different sampling, loss, regularization, or optimizer settings.

These ratio boundaries are independent stop conditions because they identify loss of the useful search distribution before every group becomes uniform. A single sub-floor measurement is noisy evidence, not mode collapse. Count only completed measurements with valid reward or optimizer telemetry. All groups becoming uniform remains an immediate stop-and-diagnose condition; mechanical and data-contract failures retain their immediate handling above.

## Training shuffle and validation

Every new calendar run must split the immutable 5,673-task source before training. Select exactly 128 validation tasks by stable hash with split seed `42`; the remaining 5,545 tasks are the full training pool. Record the source digest, split seed, row counts, and validation task IDs. Reject a launch if the full training pool and validation set overlap, their union does not reproduce all 5,673 unique source tasks, or the Daytona snapshot and `answer.txt` contracts change during partitioning.

For the 512-task short-epoch arm, select exactly 512 tasks by stable content hash with training-subset seed `42` only after creating the common validation split. The subset must be contained in the 5,545-task training pool, remain disjoint from all 128 validation tasks, and be reproducible byte-for-byte. The validation IDs must match the full-data arms exactly.

Shuffle the selected training set with Slime's `--rollout-shuffle` and `--rollout-seed 42`. The two full-data arms must use the same training data, shuffle seed, and rollout geometry so corresponding optimizer steps see the same prompt groups. The 512-task arm is a dataset-size intervention and is not step-paired with them. Do not use source-order contiguous batches for a new arm. Keep the validation set fixed and excluded from rollout training; changing any split, subset, or shuffle seed creates a new comparison and requires a new run suffix.

Evaluate all 128 validation tasks once before training and every two completed training rollouts. Use one deterministic sample per task, temperature `0`, and the same context, output, sandbox, artifact-transfer, and current-v3 verifier contracts as training. Do not set `--skip-eval-before-train`. Paired arms must use the same validation IDs, evaluation interval, and decoding settings.

The fixed validation series is the reward curve used for winner qualification and cross-arm comparison. Training-batch real reward, mixed-group retention, and entropy remain the health signals used for continuation and collapse decisions. Do not smooth, filter, or substitute training reward for a missing scheduled validation point. A missing or mechanically invalid validation run is a data-contract failure to diagnose before interpreting later points.

The active r13 jobs predate these requirements. Do not restart or retire them only to add shuffling or validation while their reward groups and entropy remain non-degenerate. Their source-ordered training rewards are diagnostic evidence, not the final smooth-curve result.

## Runtime acceptance

A launch is healthy only after all Iris replicas join one Ray cluster, all six SGLang engines start, a complete rollout is graded through fresh Daytona evaluator snapshots, optimizer step 1 has finite loss and gradient metrics, weight synchronization completes, and the next rollout begins. Scheduler `running` alone is insufficient.

Every future launch must set both `--save` and `--save-interval`. The calendar Iris driver defaults `SAVE_PATH` to `/app/checkpoints/$RUN_ID` and `SAVE_INTERVAL` to `20`; launch commands may override both explicitly but may not disable checkpointing. Slime also saves at each completed training-data epoch, so the 512-task configuration checkpoints every 16 rollouts even when that boundary does not coincide with the configured interval. Each launch must also pass `--s3-output /app/checkpoints/$RUN_ID=s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/slime/qwen3coder-calendar-v3/checkpoints/$RUN_ID` and use an S3 sync interval no longer than five minutes. All replicas mirror their globally named distributed-checkpoint shards into this one shared job prefix without deleting each other's objects. Runtime acceptance must verify the first scheduled checkpoint locally and in S3, including its tracker metadata and distributed shards, and record its iteration and S3 prefix. The active r13 arm predates this contract and must not be restarted only to add it.

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
A production-band 16-node GB200 gang on `cw-us-east-08a` has sat `SchedulingGated` for over an hour behind two batch-band 8-node jobs, because Kueue only enters preemption on quota pressure and the gang is blocked by rack topology while the fleet still has free GPUs. This is the residual of #8781: #8782 made accelerator quota binding at fleet size (`max_slices: 216`), which fixes the fleet-full case but not the rack-full case, and on a 12-rack NVL72 cluster the rack is the unit that matters.

## Observed

`/mwittmann/ra2a-8870-whl3-wh-coord/grug-train-ra2a-8870-whl3-wh` (production, 16 × gb200-4x, coscheduled on `multinode-nvlink-ib`), submitted 2026-09-04T21:17Z. Every task `building` with:

```
Kueue workload iris-pg-4b06617fd63a6fdf-0: queue=cw-use08a-lq; QuotaReserved (Pending): couldn't assign flavors to pod set e4c4e2ba: topology "multinode-nvlink-ib" allows to fit only 2 out of 16 pod(s). Total nodes: 207; excluded: resource "cpu": 192, resource "memory": 1
```

Occupancy at the time (`job_config.priority_band` from the controller DB): the hero at system on 176 nodes (11 racks × 16), and three 8-node jobs on the remainder — `/zack/exp157-rope-delta-l2-controlmatch-r5-east08-gb200-driver` **batch**, `/zack/exp177-aug-contact-order-ce-gb200-r96-driver` **batch**, `/zack/exp177-soft-target-cw-r103-…-driver` whose GPU child is production. Preempting either batch job would free 8 nodes on its rack; together with the rack's existing free nodes that is the 16 the gang needs. Kueue never evaluates it.

## Why

`ClusterQueue.preemption.withinClusterQueue: LowerPriority` is set (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/kueue_manifests.py:374`), and the design note at `:109-113` states the intent: binding accelerator quota exists "so Kueue can check whether removing lower-priority victims creates a compatible accelerator placement." But quota is derived from `max_slices` — the whole reserved fleet — so it binds only when every GPU in the cluster is allocated. With ~7 free nodes scattered across racks the workload is quota-Fit, reaches TAS, fails on topology, and is downgraded to NoFit without victim selection. Exactly the mechanism #8781 documented, one level up: fleet-level quota cannot express rack-level pressure.

The preemption events Iris *has* recorded on this cluster are from the Kubernetes scheduler (`default-scheduler: preempting to accommodate a higher priority pod`), which acts on pod priority after Kueue admission. A gang that never clears the Kueue gate never reaches it, so the system band does not help either.

## Consequence

Band semantics are inverted for the workloads the bands exist for. Any gang whose size is a rack fraction larger than the free space on the best rack queues indefinitely behind batch work, at production or system priority, while the cluster reports free capacity. On this cluster that is every EP64 job (16 of a rack's 18 nodes) whenever any other job holds more than 2 nodes on each non-hero rack.

## Possible directions

- Quota per topology domain rather than per fleet, so rack-level pressure is visible to victim selection; Kueue's TAS preemption work (kubernetes-sigs/kueue, "TAS-aware preemption") is the upstream track and #8781's install script already flags it as version-sensitive.
- Failing that, an Iris-side reclaim: when a coscheduled workload above batch reports TAS lack-of-fit for longer than a threshold, evict enough lower-band pods on the best-fitting rack to make it fit. Crude, but it restores the contract.
- At minimum, surface it: a gang gated on topology lack-of-fit with lower-band victims available should say so in `task describe`, rather than looking like ordinary queueing.

Related: #8781 (fleet-level fix, #8782), #7916 (same shape for CPU reservations on rno2a), #8247 (domain-blind placement stranding GPUs).

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

### Research

This is unintended, and the current Kueue policy cannot enforce the documented Iris band contract for topology-only pressure. Kueue defines `withinClusterQueue: LowerPriority` only for an incoming Workload that exceeds unused nominal quota; Iris enables that policy in [`build_cluster_queue`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/28d310aea26e0f44237949833652f2706a89204c/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/kueue_manifests.py#L342-L377), but [`accelerator_nominal_quotas`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/28d310aea26e0f44237949833652f2706a89204c/infra/pulumi/src/iac/coreweave/kueue.py#L46-L59) derives one fleet-wide quota from 216 physical GB200 nodes. East08's topology model guarantees only 16 schedulable nodes in each 18-node rack ([`SCHEDULABLE_RACK_NODES`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/28d310aea26e0f44237949833652f2706a89204c/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/coreweave_topology.py#L27-L50)), so a 16-node Workload can be quota-Fit and then TAS-NoFit; Kueue skips victim selection in that state.

The upstream preemption API documents quota pressure as the eligibility condition, and topology-aware priority handling remains open in [kubernetes-sigs/kueue#9992](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/issues/9992). No open Marin PR overlaps this issue.

### Proposed Fix

The smallest correct fix is topology-aware victim selection in Kueue: when a higher-priority Workload changes from quota-Fit to TAS-NoFit, evaluate lower-priority Workloads as victims and admit it when their removal creates a valid topology assignment. After upstream support exists, update Iris's Kueue pin and extend [`gpu_gang_smoke.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/28d310aea26e0f44237949833652f2706a89204c/lib/iris/tests/e2e/gpu_gang_smoke.py) with the East08 shape: two batch 8-node gangs fragment a rack, then a production 16-node gang reclaims them.

Reducing the global quota to 16/18 of physical capacity is not a correct substitute. It permanently withholds capacity that smaller workloads can use, can evict work on unrelated racks, and still cannot express which victims free a compatible domain. An Iris-side evictor would duplicate Kueue's workload lifecycle and topology snapshot; I do not recommend adding that race-prone second scheduler.

| skip first 10 | 10–47 | 6.584 | +4.49 (3.1×) |
| skip first 20 | 20–47 | 9.615 | +7.52 (4.6×) |
| skip last 10 | 0–37 | 5.455 | +3.36 (2.6×) |

Baseline reproduces the hero's logged `eval_dropless/macro_loss` at step 42k (2.094) to 0.001, so the standalone restore + reshard + dropless eval is faithful.

Every skip is catastrophic (2.6–4.6× the baseline), which cuts against the residual-decomposition read that early layers barely matter: their per-layer contribution norm is tiny (~0.01–1 vs the last-layer MLP's ~40), but removing them still breaks the loss. Small ‖Δx‖ is not removable — downstream layers were trained expecting those transformations. Two structural notes: more layers dropped is monotonically worse (skip-20 > skip-10), and skipping the first 10 hurts more than the last 10 (6.58 vs 5.45) despite the late layers carrying far larger contribution norms — the early layers build the foundation, the late layers refine it, and a missing foundation is less survivable.

W&B: `hero-12d8b6f0-skipeval-42k` (keys `skip_baseline/…`, `skip_first10/…`, `skip_first20/…`, `skip_last10/…`).

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: The first 10 layers are still critical for accurate prediction. If we zoom into the first 20 layers, we can see that the layer contribution of the first 10 layers attn is still roughly around the scale of the starting embedding. So even though the scale of the contribution pales compared to the final 10 layers, its still meaningfully changing the representation of the token.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Attention-only range knockout (dropless global macro loss, step-42000, 1 rack, 50 batches). Zeroes a contiguous range of layers' attention output before the residual add, keeping the MLPs. Compared against the whole-layer skips already posted here.

| Ablation | Global macro loss | Δ vs baseline |
|---|---|---|
| baseline | 2.093 | — |
| attn layers 0–9 zeroed (MLPs kept) | 2.798 | +0.705 |
| attn layers 38–47 zeroed (MLPs kept) | 2.436 | +0.343 |

Against the whole-layer skips (attention **and** MLP dropped):

| Range | Attn-only zeroed | Whole layer dropped |
|---|---|---|
| first 10 (0–9) | +0.705 | +4.49 (→6.58) |
| last 10 (38–47) | +0.343 | +3.36 (→5.45) |

- The MLPs carry the large majority of each range's contribution: removing only the attention in layers 0–9 costs +0.71, versus +4.49 for the whole block, so ~85% of that range's effect is the MLP path.
- Early attention matters more than late: zeroing 0–9 attention (+0.71) hurts about twice as much as 38–47 attention (+0.34), consistent with the single-layer knockout finding that no individual late-attention layer is critical.

W&B: `marin-community/marin_moe/hero-12d8b6f0-attnrangeeval-42k`

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
Summarizing findings:
1. At hero_scale attention gate shows uncharacteristic increase in norm. 
2. The 48 heads of the attention gate show high cosine similarity on any given layer. Checking layer zero, 98 percent of the time the attention gate is driving attention down to under 5 percent of its initial output scale.
3. Contributions to the residual stream scale with layer depth. MLP tends to contribute about 2x more than attention. Layer zero contributes about 1/10 the norm of the initial embed. Layer 48 contributes about 10x the norm of the initial embed. 
4. However zeroing out attention on the first 10 layers causes a meaningful increase in loss. A greater increase (2x) than zeroing out attention on the last 10 layers. So attention in early layers is still contributing very meaningfully. (changes from attention in early layers influence what updates later layers make). This contribution should act as a 'tether' that prevents these layers from becoming useless. (the gradient would yell very loudly if attention gate turned them off completely). Main learning: output scale does not correspond to impact.

Suspicion is that the attn_gate parameter has been co-opted in early layers to function as an output scaling mechanism. The intention was for the input RMSNorm on the attn block to handle this, or the sconv on attn_out.

Given that the first 10 attn layers are still critical and actively getting used (just smaller scale outputs), not viewing as issue that requires immediate action. Things would prompt intervention:
1. Loss curve slows down and no longer beats projection.
2. Ablating removing early attention layers actually shows no impact on loss later on in training.
3. We get positive results from an ablation on 1 rack that resumes from checkpoint, when compared to baseline:

Ablation ideas:
1. Update attention gate from v = 2*sigmoid(x)*v to v = (0.05 + 2*sigmoid(x))*v. Give nonzero floor.
2. Instead of hardcoded 0.05, make it a learnable bias per head with very high beta1 and beta2. Init to 0.
3. Add a general output scalar on each attn output. Init to 1 with very high beta1 and beta2.
4. Add some regularization to attn gate weight (weight decay).
5. Add hardcoded bias that ramps per step from 0 to 0.05 over 1000 steps.

All of these ablation ideas would probably not be effective as-is. But testing on 1 rack would give signal and better intuition on how the system is behaving. Since attention gate runs through a sigmoid, it would never fully decay to zero. Since this dynamic only occurs on hero scale (48 layers), all ablations would need to occur there.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
Main initial concern here was that gradient signal to the attention matrices would be getting killed by attn gate being off. But actually, the gradient signal is likely still reasonable, its just that model has adopted a behavior where output scale grows with depth (but early layers still impact prediction heavily through their impact on subsequent layers), and this depth scaling is managed partially by the attention gate, perhaps partially because matrices are under hyperball. Will be important to get per-layer gradient logging on Hero to track this more actively. (scan layers is bundling the gradient across all layers).

Traditionally the intent of residual highway is it gives direct gradient signal back from lm_head to every layer directly. However since we see output scale of every layer increase, the early layers will influence prediction very little through direct residual highway. Instead, their influence comes from how they influence subsequent layers. This seems like it would perhaps be less stable. Though training seems extremely stable so far? As long as gradient on attention matrices in initial layers looks ok, then biasing towards no action.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Layer-0 headwise attention gate, per-vocab-token (step-42000). The gate is `2·sigmoid(attn_in @ attn_gate)`, one value per head (48 heads); at layer 0 `attn_in` is a deterministic function of the token embedding, so each token has a fixed 48-head gate vector. "On" = gate > 1 (i.e. `attn_in @ attn_gate > 0`).

Layer-0 attention is near-closed by default: mean gate over the whole vocab is **0.013**. Only **546 of 128,256 tokens open ≥1 head**, and just **93 open all 48**. The tokens that stay on fall into three buckets:

**1. Reserved/special tokens (128000–128255)** — the bulk. ~200 of the 256 special tokens open all 48 heads (opensum 96/96): `<|reserved_special_token_*|>` plus the structural specials (`<|begin_of_text|>`, `<|end_of_text|>`, `<|eot_id|>`).

**2. Malformed / byte-fragment real-vocab tokens** — the top non-special tokens are almost all junk:
- undecodable UTF-8 byte fragments that decode to `�` (ids 124, 125, 178–187), several at the full 96/96
- rare foreign-script subwords: Turkish (`ıldığında`, `ılmaz`, `uştur`, `ılmaktadır`), Cyrillic/Ukrainian (`уватися`, `илася`, `аракт`), Czech (`ujícím`), CJK spam strings (`菲律宾申博`, `갤로그로`)
- gibberish/spam: `eoqkrvldkf`, `.:.:.:.:.:.:`, `.**************`, `ЎыџN`

**3. Ordinary English text tokens** — essentially none; common words sit at gate ≈ 0.

Distribution of open-head counts (real-vocab tokens only, excluding the special block): 345 open ≥1 head, 32 open ≥12 heads.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: Hmm the MLP router follows a similar scaling trajectory, diverging from the scaling ladder. A light weight decay on these two parameters would be relatively low risk and increase how learnable they are later on in training. The prior 67B-10T tokens had similar router growth and trained perfectly fine with zero loss spikes. However it didn't show this attn_gate behavior. Feeling more optimistic on weight decay on these two parameters. Will run some experiments to collect more data. Smaller magnitude attn_gate will mean it can do less rescaling in early layers, but the rms norm weight should be able to pick up this behavior. Low-opinionated form of WD would scale it via lr/peak_lr, so it doesn't impact end of training dynamics.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Weight-decay ablation on the attn_gate / router weights (motivated by the router-norm growth vs small router-z-loss noted above). Decoupled AdamW-style wd applied only to the attn_gate and/or router weight leaves (router_bias, embeddings, norm gains untouched). H100 scaling-ladder rungs, dropless eval.

## d768 (16 H100, batch 1024, 11,420 steps — all finished)

Final dropless paloma macro loss (and overall macro across all eval tags):

| run | wd on gate+router | paloma macro | overall macro | Δ paloma vs base |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 0 | 3.0158 | 2.8352 | — |
| wd 0.01 const | 0.01 | 3.0185 | 2.8372 | +0.0027 |
| wd 0.1 const | 0.1 | 3.0158 | 2.8348 | +0.0000 |
| wd 0.1 -> 0 linear | 0.1 decay | **3.0150** | **2.8344** | -0.0008 |
| wd 0.04, hold 15% then 0.0425 -> 0 | partial | 3.0182 | 2.8370 | +0.0024 |

Takeaway: at d768 the effect is negligible (all within ~0.003, ~0.1%, i.e. eval noise). The 0.1->0 linear decay is marginally best on both paloma and overall; the weaker/partial schedules (0.01 constant, 0.04-hold15) are marginally worse. No schedule hurt training, none clearly helped.

## d1024 (32 H100, batch 2048, 15,276 steps — still running)

Head-to-head at the latest common eval step (7,639 / 50%). wd here is the hold-15%-then-0.0425->0 schedule; the two runs differ only in whether it also decays the router weight.

| run | wd target | paloma macro @7639 | overall macro @7639 |
|---|---|---|---|
| d1024_baseline | none | 2.9778 | 2.8016 |
| gate only | attn_gate | 2.9801 | 2.8031 |
| gate + router | attn_gate + router | **2.9778** | **2.8012** |

Also within noise so far (~0.002 spread). gate+router edges out baseline; gate-only is marginally worse. Current steps: baseline 7.7k, gate 10.5k, gate+router 8.4k (offsets from a one-time cold kernel-compile stall); comparison is pinned to the last step all three share. Will update at completion.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: All runs within noise. But do constrain the norm somewhat. Impact on scale will probably be larger on hero since attn_gate scale has already grown so much.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 d1024 weight-decay ablation — final (all three finished at step 15,276; 32 H100, batch 2048; dropless eval). wd schedule on the targeted leaves: 0 for the first 15% of training, then the 0.05·(1−step/N) line (0.0425 at the 15% mark) decaying to 0. Same seed; differ only in the decay target.

| run | wd target | paloma macro | overall macro | Δ paloma vs base |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| d1024_baseline | none | 2.7799 | 2.5982 | — |
| gate only | attn_gate | 2.7797 | 2.5979 | -0.0002 |
| gate + router | attn_gate + router | **2.7777** | **2.5964** | -0.0022 |

Takeaway: consistent with d768 — the effect is small (within ~0.002). gate+router edges out baseline on both metrics; gate-only is indistinguishable from baseline. No schedule hurt training. So decaying the router weight (on top of the gate) gives the small, consistent improvement; the attention gate alone does essentially nothing.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 attn_gate logit scaling — dropless eval on the step-48000 hero checkpoint (d6144, 1 rack, expert-collapsed dropless mesh, 50 batches × 64 seq per paloma tag).

Applies a scalar multiplier to the headwise attn_gate logits before the sigmoid: `gate = 2·sigmoid(scale · (x @ attn_gate))`. `scale<1` shrinks the logits toward 0, relaxing every head's gate toward the neutral 1.0; `scale=0` removes the learned headwise gating entirely (all gates = 1.0).

| attn_gate logit scale | dropless macro loss |
|---|---|
| 1.0 (baseline) | 2.0875 |
| 0.8 | 2.0973 |
| 0.6 | 2.7852 |
| 0.4 | 8.4599 |
| 0.2 | 9.8986 |
| 0.0 | 9.3836 |

Shrinking the gate logits by 20% is nearly free (+0.010). The model degrades at 0.6 and collapses at 0.4 and below — the learned headwise gating is load-bearing, and its effect is concentrated in the top ~40% of the logit magnitude. (The 0.2 < 0.0 non-monotonicity is inside the already-collapsed regime.)

Caveat: the `paloma/macro_loss` sub-aggregate came back `nan` for every ablation including the unaltered baseline, so it's an eval-set aggregation artifact unrelated to the scaling; the table reports the overall dropless macro across all resolved eval tags.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: Model degrades heavily if attn_gate scale is dropped by 50%. It seems quite reliant on this parameter right now. Given loss curve and evals all look super stable, I dont think we are in a rush to collapse the norms quickly. 0.03 WD can still halve the norms over 9k steps, and bring everything to a reasonable level scale for later parts of training. So see very little downside to starting with a more conservative 0.03 WD, then ramping later if needed.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
One interesting data point here: 
"Pre-training (MAI-Base-1): AdamW with a constant weight decay of 0.1, with reduced weight decay on attention weights (0.01) and embedding weights (0.005) to limit regularization on parameters that benefit less from it."
Seems that a range of decay weights are used in practice.

comments.author: Mooler0410
comments.body: This might be related to what we found in our ultra-sparse MoE training (768 experts / top-8, 60B and 180B); the write-up is here: [https://alltoall.notion.site/save-lower-layer-moe-experts-llal](https://alltoall.notion.site/save-lower-layer-moe-experts-llal) In our runs the routed experts of the **first few MoE layers stop learning** after a few thousand steps, while the shared expert stays healthy and loss / evals / load balance all look normal. We trained with AdamW, weight decay and the default ε, so it showed up as weight-norm collapse in those layers. With Muon, or with a very small ε, the norms look fine but the layers still stop learning (momentum in those layers drops ~3 orders of magnitude, and masking their routed experts barely changes downstream metrics) — unless we give them an extra informative signal during a critical period at the start of training (an aux LM loss on the first MoE layer for the first 2–4k steps). Alongside this we saw the early-layer attention stop learning too, which makes sense: if the MLP stops adding meaningful representation to the residual, there is nothing stable for attention to build on. In our runs the order was clearly MLP first, attention as a consequence. Your setup is very different from ours (MuonH with hyperball, latent MoE, headwise attention gates, QB, no dense layers), so we're only saying this might be the same thing. **We also don't know what happens at 18T tokens — our longest run in this blog is 2T, and there every collapsed layer except the first MoE layer had either recovered or was starting to by the end; the first one stayed dead.** What you are seeing in layer 0 — attention gated shut for essentially every ordinary token, diverging from the ladder at ~1% into the run — looks like the attention side of the same thing. And in the per-layer watch from ra2a-evaldl-c3f51 (48k checkpoint) we also see the abnormally small gradients on the **layer-0/1 routed experts: w_gate/w_up/w_down at 2.4e-5 / 2.4e-5 / 6.0e-5 in layer 0, 200–430× below layers 5–19 and ~100× below the layer-0 shared expert,** while the shared experts and attention in the same layer are normal; layer 1 is ~10× low, layers 2–4 look fine. One cheap check would settle it: **routed-expert-only masking (probably free ? ).**

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: > This might be related to what we found in our ultra-sparse MoE training (768 experts / top-8, 60B and 180B); the write-up is here: https://alltoall.notion.site/save-lower-layer-moe-experts-llal Great blog! I think our early attention layers are still learning fine, just using a somewhat awkward mechanism (the attention gate) to manage their scale. But what you found- the dead gradient in first 2 layers, does probably indicate those routed experts are not contributing. Updated grads: I love your idea of starting training with a temporary aux loss. At this stage, I think interventions midrun are probably not worthwhile for those 2 layers. Doubling the number of routed parameters is equivalent to the gain of training on 20% more tokens, when measured near compute optimal. So losing 2 layers of routed experts, (4% of routed params), is probably very marginal impact on model quality (part of this is also because we have atypically large shared experts). But maybe after the pretrain run we could just remove them, or try some experiments on intermittent checkpoints for science purposes.

comments.author: Mooler0410
comments.body:
Agree. We did something similar to our main model after the run finished😆, since we found this problem midway through training. This did not cause any fatal issues in our main run. 

Looking forward to more interesting findings!

| Hero with token dropping, step 45,837 | 0.8868 |

### Current 15-subset UncheatableEval

| Model | BPB |
|---|---:|
| Nemotron 3 Ultra-550B-A55B-Base | 0.4663 |
| DeepSeek V4 Flash Base | 0.4678 |
| Kimi K2 Base | 0.4781 |
| Nemotron 3 Super-120B-A12B-Base | 0.4964 |
| Arcee Trinity Large Base | 0.5244 |
| Gemma 4 26B-A4B | 0.5345 |
| Seed OSS 36B Base | 0.5422 |
| Nemotron 3 Nano-30B-A3B-Base | 0.5703 |
| OLMo 3 32B Base | 0.5821 |

### Earlier 7-subset UncheatableEval

| Model | BPB |
|---|---:|
| Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base | 0.5245 |
| Hero without token dropping, step 45,837 | 0.5362 |
| Hero with token dropping, step 45,837 | 0.6220 |

The 7-subset and 15-subset UncheatableEval values are not directly comparable.

Each subset forecast fits BPB as a function of Paloma macro loss across 77 paired ladder measurements. It then applies the preregistered macro-loss scaling law. Fifteen fits have `R² ≥ 0.997`; Twitter AAE has `R² = 0.971`.

The FLOP axis uses `6 × active parameters × training tokens` estimates. Nano is at `5.25e23` FLOPs. Qwen is at `6.48e23` FLOPs, assuming 3B active parameters and 36T tokens. OLMo is at `1.06e24` FLOPs from 32B parameters and 5.50T tokens. Trinity is at about `1.33e24` FLOPs, assuming 13B active parameters and 17T tokens. Super is at least `1.8e24` FLOPs because NVIDIA reports more than 25T training tokens. Flash is at least `2.50e24` FLOPs from 13B active parameters and more than 32T tokens. Seed is at `2.59e24` FLOPs from 36B parameters and 12T tokens. Kimi is at about `2.98e24` FLOPs, using 32B active parameters and 15.5T tokens. Ultra is at about `6.6e24` FLOPs, assuming 55B active parameters and about 20T tokens. Gemma's training token count is unknown, so plots show it as a dashed reference line. Exact FLOPs for the hybrid MoE models are unknown.

A bootstrap over the four ladder runs gives 0.7404–0.7432 macro BPB. This range covers the loss-to-BPB conversion, not error in the loss forecast.

The forecast assumes a 4K context, the original data mix, and the planned token count. These inputs can change before training ends. Training-data overlap with the evaluation sets is unknown. We do not have a final UncheatableEval forecast.

spillover_issues.title: Compare Marin's Hero run to open-weight base models on PPL

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
## Description

Splash Attention supports static causal/local masks and runtime segment IDs, but prefix-LM with packed, data-dependent prefixes needs structured block skipping to avoid dense mask fallbacks at long context lengths. This experiment tracks prefix-LM Splash lowering, packed prefix masks, and the path toward segment-ID/THD-style block skipping.

<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

Packed prefix-LM support and pure causal packed segment-ID Splash block skipping are implemented on `codex/splash-prefixlm-block-skipping`. The compact gather fix resolves the major v5p regression: at 16384, packed prefix-LM improved from `110.432 ms` to about `4.5 ms`, and packed causal segment improved from `110.357 ms` to about `4.4 ms` on v5p-8. v5e and v6e parity/benchmark validation also passes, and packed segment/prefix-LM beats dense references at 8192 on both families. Direct segment-run metadata is correctness-preserving but still slower than generic packed segment metadata, especially on B=2 Alpaca-style many-doc layouts. Do not promote segment-run metadata as the default packed causal path yet.

### Helpful links
- Draft PR: #6330
- Research logbook: `.agents/logbooks/splash-prefixlm-block-skipping.md`
- Handoff: `.agents/projects/splash-prefixlm-block-skipping-handoff.md`
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Scope

* Support static prefix-LM, dynamic prefix lengths, and packed `prefix_mask + segment_ids` without regressing existing Splash masks.
* Add pure causal packed segment-ID block skipping for `AttentionMask.causal(segment_ids=...)`.
* Compare against dense/reference attention at 8192 and 16384 on v4-8 and v5p-8.
* Continue toward compact segment-run metadata for packed segment-ID masks, then check v5e/v6e compatibility.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Structured mask metadata can skip empty Splash blocks for prefix-LM and packed docs without a major steady-state speed hit, and the same representation can lead toward THD-style packed attention.

### Links

* Research logbook: `.agents/logbooks/splash-prefixlm-block-skipping.md`
* Draft PR: #6330
* Benchmark harness: `lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_splash_attention_masks.py`
* Handoff: `.agents/projects/splash-prefixlm-block-skipping-handoff.md`

## Current baseline

B=1, S=8192 or 16384, H=8, D=128, bf16, block size 512, four packed docs per sequence. v5p/v5e/v6e runs use scoped VMEM settings where applicable.

## Results

v5p-8 at direct segment-run builder commit `11b762201`, 8192 with dense references: static causal `1.217 ms`; packed causal segment `1.795 ms`; packed segment-runs `3.385 ms`; packed prefix-LM `1.774 ms`; dense references `1.866-1.900 ms`.

v5p-8 at direct segment-run builder commit `11b762201`, 16384 Splash-only: static causal `3.293 ms`; packed causal segment `4.402 ms`; packed segment-runs `6.619 ms`; packed prefix-LM `4.487 ms`.

v5p-8 B=2 Alpaca-style packed layouts at `11b762201`, 8192 with dense references: static causal `1.200 ms`; packed causal segment `1.692 ms`; packed segment-runs `9.352 ms`; packed prefix-LM `1.755 ms`; dense references `1.857-1.870 ms`.

v5e (`v5litepod-8`) at `7c80f737`, 8192 with dense references: static causal `2.043 ms`; packed causal segment `3.965 ms`; packed segment-runs `6.114 ms`; packed prefix-LM `3.947 ms`; dense references `5.474-5.485 ms`. 16384 Splash-only: static causal `6.186 ms`; packed causal segment `11.074 ms`; packed segment-runs `11.881 ms`; packed prefix-LM `11.196 ms`.

v6e-8 at `7c80f737`, 8192 with dense references: static causal `1.841 ms`; packed causal segment `2.768 ms`; packed segment-runs `5.092 ms`; packed prefix-LM `2.884 ms`; dense references `3.221-3.250 ms`. 16384 Splash-only: static causal `5.488 ms`; packed causal segment `7.622 ms`; packed segment-runs `10.273 ms`; packed prefix-LM `7.686 ms`.

v5p-8 pre-fix regression at `d907d856`: packed causal segment `110.357 ms` and packed prefix-LM `110.432 ms` at 16384. The compact gather fix removes that regression.

v4-8 after direct blocked metadata, 8192 with dense references: packed causal segment Splash steady median `1.537 ms` versus dense `3.763 ms`; packed prefix-LM Splash steady median `1.547 ms` versus dense `3.756 ms`; static causal Splash steady median `1.844 ms`.

v4-8 after direct blocked metadata, 16384 Splash-only: static causal `5.795 ms`; packed causal segment `4.462 ms`; packed prefix-LM `4.445 ms`.

Dynamic prefix-length, packed prefix-mask, and packed causal segment-ID TPU-gated tests pass on v4/v5p/v5e/v6e evidence. Local metadata tests cover ragged packed documents, compact partial payloads, fixed-shape segment-run metadata, inactive padded segment slots, and many-short-doc layouts. At latest head `28ec236ac`, changed-file precommit passed and lint review reported no findings.

## Decision log

* 2026-06-11: Use dev TPU for fast kernel iteration; confirm final claims on PR CI and target TPU families.
* 2026-06-11: Represent packed prefix-LM as `prefix_mask + segment_ids`, with Splash metadata encoding same-segment filtering.
* 2026-06-12: Add first pure causal packed segment-ID block skipping via dynamic Splash metadata.
* 2026-06-12: Add a repeatable benchmark harness and record v4-8 8192/16384 numbers.
* 2026-06-12: Confirm the same benchmark shape on v5p-8; packed Splash beats dense references and static causal Splash for packed docs.
* 2026-06-12: Replace packed-mask dense SxS metadata construction with direct blocked metadata; v4-8 rerun preserves performance.
* 2026-06-12: Replace broadcast/reduce compact block selection with direct `nonzero` + gather; v5p rerun fixes the 16384 packed prefix/segment regression.
* 2026-06-12: Build segment-run metadata directly from contiguous document intervals; local correctness/lint gates pass.
* 2026-06-12: Direct segment-run v5p timing does not improve steady state; keep segment-run metadata opt-in/experimental and investigate metadata shape/schedule overhead before promoting it.
* 2026-06-12: v5e/v6e compatibility confirmed for packed segment and prefix-LM block-skipping paths.

## Negative results index

* 2026-06-12: Direct-commit v5p rerun was capacity-blocked earlier in the day and fell back to v4-8.
* 2026-06-12: `GAIR/lima` direct HF loading failed locally because the installed `datasets` package rejects dataset scripts; use local JSONL or a script-free mirror for LIMA-style lengths.
* 2026-06-12: Direct segment-run metadata remains slower than generic packed segment metadata on v5p: `6.619 ms` versus `4.402 ms` at 16384, and `9.352 ms` versus `1.692 ms` on B=2 Alpaca-style 8192 layouts.

| 32768 | packed causal segment | 1 | 544/4096 | 86.719% | 14.743 ms | 14.743 ms | 1.23x slower |
| 32768 | static causal | 20 | 2080/4096 | 49.219% | 226.294 ms | 11.315 ms | 1.00x |
| 32768 | packed causal segment | 20 | 544/4096 | 86.719% | 137.467 ms | 6.873 ms | 1.65x faster |

Interpretation: the current dynamic packed causal segment path is slower for single-layer calls, but with prepared-plan reuse across a 20-layer stack it becomes clearly faster at both 16K and 32K. Effective visited blocks are `27.27%` of static causal at 16K and `26.15%` at 32K; realized speedups are smaller than block-count reduction because the dynamic metadata path still has overhead. Compile-including cost is also the main caveat: packed causal segment compile-including was `39.78 s` at 16K/20 layers and `158.28 s` at 32K/20 layers; 32K lowering warned about `3.22GB` captured constants.

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
## Description
Levanter TPU serving now splits OpenAI service batches by aggregate prompt-token budget, which fixes dropped long-prompt requests when total prompt tokens exceed one prefill admission. The remaining mixed workload gap is performance: `mixed_b32_i512_o512_n1` on v6e-8 completes correctly after PR #6176, but serializes the 32 long-prompt requests into four 8-request engine batches and reaches about 0.326 of vLLM decode throughput.

Add engine-level support for admitting or overlapping multiple prefill chunks for one logical service batch so long-prompt mixed RL rollout workloads remain correct without full service-batch serialization.

### Definition of Done
- `mixed_b32_i512_o512_n1` on Qwen3-8B v6e-8 completes all 16384 expected completion tokens with no no-progress warnings under default prefill settings.
- The long-prompt mixed workload reaches at least 0.75 of the matching vLLM-TPU decode throughput, or the remaining gap is explained by a measured kernel/device limit rather than service-batch serialization.
- Tests cover batches whose aggregate prompt tokens exceed one `max_prefill_size` admission.
- Benchmark output reports enough admission/chunking metrics to distinguish service serialization from device decode throughput.

Part of #1898

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read repo guides + skill docs
- [x] Verify issue is actionable (DoD is concrete)
- [x] Locate root cause in engine prefill/admission path
- [x] Check open work (PR #6176 is the merged/pending service-layer split this issue follows up on)
- [x] Post research + proposed approach
- [ ] Hand off to human for design sign-off before implementation (scope > 100 LOC)

# Research

`engine.generate()` admits prompts **exactly once** per call: it builds one `PrefillWork` sized to `max_prefill_size`, then loops decoding until done. Once `_prefill_prompts` packs `max_prefill_size` tokens (or `max_seqs_in_prefill` requests), the request loop `break`s — remaining requests are returned to the queue but never admitted within that `generate()` call. PR #6176's service-layer split (\`_max_prompt_tokens_per_batch = max_prefill_size\`) hides the correctness bug by feeding the engine at most one prefill's worth of requests per call, which fully serializes \`mixed_b32_i512_o512_n1\` into 4 × 8-request \`generate()\` calls and reaches only 0.326 of vLLM decode throughput. The triage doc at [docs/debug-log-qwen3-mixed-progress.md](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/qwen3-dense-parity-matrix/docs/debug-log-qwen3-mixed-progress.md) walks the diagnosis (single-admission ⇒ 8/32 requests served ⇒ 2 zero-progress iters ⇒ bail-out).

**Relevant code**
- [\`engine.py#L1143-L1148\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/inference/engine.py#L1143-L1148) — single \`_prefill_batch(requests)\` then decode loop
- [\`engine.py#L971-L985\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/inference/engine.py#L971-L985) — \`_prefill_prompts\` breaks when next request overflows \`max_prefill_size\`
- [\`engine.py#L911-L926\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/inference/engine.py#L911-L926) — \`_prefill_batch\` wraps one \`_run_prefill\`
- [\`openai.py#L183-L189\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/qwen3-dense-parity-matrix/lib/levanter/src/levanter/inference/openai.py#L183-L189) — service-layer cap that this issue wants to relax (PR #6176)
- [\`engine.py#L1159-L1225\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/inference/engine.py#L1159-L1225) — decode loop with no re-admission hook

# Proposed Approach (design review needed; not implementing)

Move admission from a one-shot before-decode step to an admission **driver inside the decode loop**, so one logical service batch can be admitted across multiple prefill calls interleaved with decode rounds.

Sketch:

1. **\`generate()\` keeps a pending queue.** Replace the single \`_prefill_batch(requests)\` call with a \`pending = deque(requests)\` plus a small helper \`_try_admit(pending) -> _DecodeOutputs | None\` that pops requests off \`pending\` until the next \`PrefillWork\` is full (same accounting as today: \`max_prefill_size\`, \`max_seqs_in_prefill\`, \`free_slots\`, \`n_generations\`). Initial admission becomes the first \`_try_admit\` call.

2. **Decode loop calls \`_try_admit\` per iteration** before \`_run_generation_loop\`, only when \`pending\` is non-empty and there are free slots. Each admission is one extra \`_run_prefill\` (already JIT-compiled for the existing \`(max_prefill_size, max_seqs_in_prefill)\` shapes — no new traces). Newly-admitted sequences join the active decode set on the next round.

3. **Drop the service-layer aggregate cap from PR #6176** (keep the per-request \`> max_prefill_size\` reject, since that case still cannot fit). \`_request_fits_batch\` no longer gates on \`prompt_tokens()\`; the engine handles overflow via chunked admission.

4. **Metrics.** Add to \`GenerationResult\` (or a sibling \`GenerationStats\`): \`num_prefill_admissions\`, \`prompt_tokens_per_admission: list[int]\`, \`decode_iters_with_concurrent_admission: int\`. Surface them through the benchmark harness so the report can distinguish service serialization from device decode throughput (DoD bullet 4).

5. **Tests** in \`tests/inference/test_engine.py\`: a batch with aggregate prompt tokens \`> max_prefill_size\` must (a) complete all expected tokens, (b) report \`num_prefill_admissions > 1\`, (c) not hit the no-progress bail-out. Add a smaller-scale CPU/parity variant (e.g. 8 seqs × 64 tok with \`max_prefill_size=128\`) so it runs in normal CI.

**Open design questions for human review** (do not want to guess these):

- **Capacity gating for admission.** Today \`max_pages\` and \`max_seqs\` size the cache up-front. Should mid-decode admission be gated on a measured free-pages count, or do we keep the current static \`free_slots\` check and rely on the existing \`max_seqs\` envelope?
- **Stop-token / config shape mismatch.** When a later admission inside the same \`generate()\` call carries different stop-token shapes than the first, do we fail loud (current behavior at lines 1129-1141) or pre-validate the whole queue once before the loop?
- **Per-call back-pressure.** Should \`generate()\` keep its current "process every request passed in" contract, or take an \`InferenceContext\`-style budget and return un-admitted requests for the caller to retry? The former is simpler; the latter matches how vLLM exposes admission to its scheduler.
- **Performance ceiling.** DoD asks for ≥0.75× vLLM decode throughput. With chunked admission, the 4 prefill chunks remain serial relative to each other but overlap with decode. On v6e-8 \`mixed_b32_i512_o512_n1\` the prefill chunks are ~tens of ms and decode rounds are similar — expect a meaningful win over 0.326 but it is worth a quick back-of-envelope before committing. If the gap remains, the next step is decode-during-prefill kernel work, which is a separate epic.

Scope estimate: ~150-300 LOC across \`engine.py\`, \`openai.py\`, and a new test, plus a benchmark wiring change. Above the 100-LOC PR threshold — flagging for human approval on the design (especially the four questions above) before I open a branch.

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
We want to make Iris more natively multi-backend. It currently supports k8s (via "direct provider") & GCP, but doesn't have a strong boundary for what a "provider" should provide.

As we would like to be able to integrate with Slurm clusters soon, let's use this as an opportunity to more clearly articulate the layering and role of Iris in such an environment. Specifically, we want Iris to provide a consistent submission and monitoring interface on top of one or _more_ backends (only 1 backend is supported today).

Some backends, like K8S provide scheduling, monitoring, autoscaling & execution themselves. Others, like the default GCP/TPU backend require Iris to supply all of this functionality.

My rough pitch would be to clearly define a `backend` contract (which we will have to detangle from the existing GCP implementation detail of "backend"). The Iris controller would then be responsible for polling backends for status and updating job state.

The top-level scheduling loop in Iris would "meta-schedule" -  fetch pending jobs, and for each backend, identify the appropriate label (based on some constraint like "backend=slurm-stanford"), then ask the backend to attempt scheduling. Similarly, backends would be queried for node status and rolled up into a composite system picture.

We'll want to approach this in phases: first defining a more coherent backend contract, refactoring backend-specific code like the current node-scheduler, adjusting the top-level controller to invoke a single-backend schedule & reconcile loop, add slurm support as a new backend, and finally introducing multi-backend support.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue and confirm scope (architectural; multi-phase design)
- [x] Map current backend boundary in `lib/iris/`
- [x] Check for duplicate work (no open PRs/issues for Slurm)
- [x] Post Research + Proposed Approach (no PR — too large for one)
- [ ] Await human review of the proposed phased plan before any implementation

# Research

The "backend" boundary is currently split across three unrelated abstractions and one `isinstance(K8sTaskProvider)` branch in the controller. There is no single "backend" contract a Slurm implementation could fill: scheduling, worker daemons, capacity provisioning, and status polling are all wired differently between the GCP/TPU path and the K8s path.

Two execution models exist today, distinguished by `isinstance(self._provider, K8sTaskProvider)`:
- **Iris-scheduled (GCP, manual, local)** — `Scheduler` matches tasks→workers, `Autoscaler` provisions slices, worker daemons execute, `TaskProvider` dispatches via Connect RPC, `_run_polling_loop` reconciles.
- **Backend-scheduled (K8s/CoreWeave)** — no scheduler, no autoscaler, no worker daemon; `_run_direct_provider_loop` drains PENDING rows, the provider applies pods, Kueue admits, and the provider sync polls k8s for status. The `Scheduler` is bypassed entirely.

A Slurm backend looks much closer to the K8s path (Slurm owns scheduling and capacity) than the GCP path, so the immediate refactor is not "add a backend" but "give the two existing models a single, named protocol."

**Relevant code**
- [`controller/provider.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/provider.py) — `TaskProvider` Protocol; RPC fan-out to worker daemons only
- [`controller/direct_provider.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/direct_provider.py) — K8s-shaped drain/sync types living in the controller package
- [`controller/controller.py#L286,L345,L529,L793,L1508`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/controller.py#L286) — `TaskProvider | K8sTaskProvider` union + four `isinstance` branches
- [`providers/protocols.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/providers/protocols.py) — `ControllerProvider`/`WorkerInfraProvider` (infra lifecycle, not task execution)
- [`providers/factory.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/providers/factory.py) — `workers=None` for CoreWeave already encodes the "backend manages workers" case

# Proposed Approach

Adopt the issue author's phasing. I would not open a PR yet — each phase is large enough to deserve its own review. Sketch below; happy to write a `.agents/projects/2026MMDD_iris_backend_contract.md` design doc if this direction is approved.

**Phase 1 — name the contract.** Introduce one `Backend` protocol that explicitly enumerates the axes today's `isinstance` branches encode. Strawman:

```python
class Backend(Protocol):
    name: str                       # e.g. "gcp", "coreweave", "slurm-stanford"
    selector: dict[str, str]        # constraint match, e.g. {"backend": "slurm-stanford"}

    # Scheduling model — who picks the node?
    scheduling: Literal["iris", "backend"]

    # Per-tick reconcile entry points; implementations no-op what they don't own.
    def sync_tasks(self, batch: DirectProviderBatch) -> DirectProviderSyncResult: ...
    def dispatch_to_workers(self, plans: list[WorkerReconcilePlan], ...) -> list[ReconcileResult]: ...
    def ping_workers(self, workers: list[tuple[WorkerId, str | None]]) -> list[PingResult]: ...
    def capacity(self) -> ClusterCapacity | None: ...
    def close(self) -> None: ...
```

`TaskProvider` (RPC fan-out) and `K8sTaskProvider` become two `Backend` impls; the controller's `isinstance` checks collapse to `backend.scheduling == "backend"` and dispatch through one interface. `DirectProviderBatch`/`SyncResult`/`SchedulingEvent`/`ClusterCapacity` move out of `controller/direct_provider.py` into a backend-neutral module.

**Phase 2 — detangle the node-scheduler.** `Scheduler` + `Autoscaler` + `WorkerProvider` are coupled by the GCP-VM lifecycle. Split them so the autoscaler depends on `WorkerInfraProvider` (already a protocol) and the scheduler runs only when `backend.scheduling == "iris"`. The current `_sync_direct_provider` and `_run_scheduling_loop` become two callable phases the controller invokes per backend.

**Phase 3 — single-backend controller refactor.** Replace the two parallel loops in `controller.py` with one loop that asks each registered backend to (a) sync its tasks and (b) report capacity, rolling status up into the existing `tasks`/`workers` tables. Still single-backend; just no `isinstance`.

**Phase 4 — Slurm backend.** Implement `SlurmBackend` with `scheduling="backend"`: `sbatch` for dispatch, `squeue`/`sacct` for poll, no Iris worker daemon (workers in Slurm jobs talk to controller for log/state RPCs like CoreWeave pods do). Open questions for the human: do we want a worker daemon inside the allocation (closer to GCP path, lets us reuse `WorkerProvider` RPC fan-out), or direct task launch via sbatch (closer to K8s path)? The latter is simpler; the former lets users `iris exec` into a Slurm allocation.

**Phase 5 — multi-backend.** Make `Controller.__init__` accept `list[Backend]`. Scheduling loop iterates backends, asks each to schedule any pending tasks whose constraints match its `selector`. Capacity rollup unions per-backend `ClusterCapacity`. Reconcile fan-out queries each backend in parallel.

Sizing: Phase 1 alone is ~300–500 LOC of moves + ~10 callsite updates and is the prerequisite for everything else. Phases 2–3 are likely 500–1000 LOC each. Phase 4 is a green-field backend implementation. Phase 5 is small once 1–3 land. I'd suggest the first PR be Phase 1 only.

If this phasing looks right, I can take Phase 1 next: define the `Backend` protocol, move the backend-neutral types out of `controller/direct_provider.py`, and replace the `isinstance` checks. Tagging for human review before any code lands.
